lesson.subtitle: Lesson 26 -- Projects: Deadlines and Deliverables (By, Until, Before, After)
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rafael Gasparelli Lima | Lesson 26 -- On Track or Behind Schedule?
lesson.grammar_point: time prepositions for deadlines: by vs until, before and after + time or -ing

listenings.text: Why do so many projects finish late? Usually, the problem starts on day one. First, write every task on a list, with a name and a date. A date is not a wish. If you say by Friday, the task must be finished on Friday or before. Second, check the progress every week. Don't wait until the end of the month to find a problem. Third, look at the workload. If one person has ten tasks, the project will be behind schedule. And finally, if you need more time, ask for an extension early, before the deadline, not after it. Clients don't like surprises. A project that is on track is not a miracle: it's a habit.

Hi Rafael, it's Paulo. I'm calling about the new farms project. I'm sorry, but we're a little behind schedule. The rain didn't stop until last Thursday, so the team couldn't work in the fields for ten days. Our plan was to finish the irrigation system by October fifteenth. Now I think we can finish it by the end of October. Can we ask the board for a two-week extension? The good news is that the rest of the project is on track. The workers will plant the first trees after the irrigation is ready, and before the summer starts. I'll send you the full progress report before Friday's meeting. Talk soon.

extra_audio.text: First, the team writes every task on a list, with a name and a date. Then, they check the progress every Monday morning. Next, they see that one task is behind schedule because of the rain. After that, Rafael asks the client for a short extension before the deadline. Finally, the team submits the last deliverable by the new date.
